to: very large models on modest data, stopped before convergence
description: Kaplan et al. 2020: for a fixed compute budget, train very large models on a relatively modest amount of data and stop well before convergence.
evidence: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models: optimally compute-efficient training involves training very large models on a relatively modest amount of data and stopping significantly before convergence

to: scale model size and training tokens equally
description: Hoffmann et al. 2022: current models are undertrained; for every doubling of model size, double the training tokens (Chinchilla, 70B, 4x more data than Gopher).
evidence: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models: for every doubling of model size the number of training tokens should also be doubled

to: repeat data for up to 4 epochs
description: Muennighoff et al. 2023: with limited unique data, up to 4 epochs of repeated data changes loss negligibly; with more repetition the value of extra compute decays to zero.
evidence: Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models: training with up to 4 epochs of repeated data yields negligible changes to loss compared to having unique data

to: train smaller and longer than chinchilla-optimal when inference demand is large
description: Sardana et al. 2023: once inference cost is counted, expecting large inference demand (~1B requests) favours smaller models trained longer than Chinchilla-optimal. This revises the 2022 advice for models that will serve heavy inference; it does not test the 2022 fit itself.
evidence: Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal: Accounting for Inference in Language Model Scaling Laws: should train models smaller and longer than Chinchilla-optimal

description: Hoffmann et al. 2022 proposed three methods to estimate the compute-optimal scaling law; the third fits a parametric loss function. (Date of the Hoffmann paper; wording from the 2024 replication.)
evidence: Chinchilla Scaling: A replication attempt: Hoffmann et al. (2022) propose three methods for estimating a compute-optimal scaling law.

to: disputed by replication; refit agrees with approaches 1 and 2
description: Besiroglu et al. 2024: the published approach-3 estimates are inconsistent with approaches 1 and 2, fail to fit the extracted data and report implausibly narrow intervals; their refit agrees with approaches 1 and 2.
evidence: Chinchilla Scaling: A replication attempt: our rederivation of the scaling law using the third approach yields results that are compatible with the findings from the first two estimation procedures

to: abilities present only in larger models that extrapolation cannot predict
description: Wei et al. 2022 describe emergence as an unpredictable phenomenon of larger models.
evidence: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models: emergent abilities cannot be predicted simply by extrapolating the performance of smaller models

to: artifact of the researcher's choice of metric
description: Schaeffer et al. 2023 offer an alternative explanation: nonlinear or discontinuous metrics create the jump. Both explanations remain in the literature; this entry does not close the 2022 one.
evidence: Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?: emergent abilities appear due to the researcher's choice of metric rather than due to fundamental changes in model behavior with scale
